findings.fix: Set lang to the actual document language, for example lang="en".
findings.violation: The lang attribute is not a valid language code, so assistive technology cannot determine the page's language and may mispronounce content or fail to load the correct voice or braille table.

findings.fix: Give the page a descriptive title, for example "Rider service updates".
findings.violation: The title element is empty, so the browser tab, bookmarks, and screen reader page announcement all have no descriptive name for the page.

findings.evidence: Both paragraphs end with the sentence "Station staff can also help with the same request in person."
findings.fix: Write a distinct, accurate closing sentence for each paragraph, or remove the redundant one.
findings.violation: The same closing sentence is reused for two unrelated requests, fare adjustment and checking real time arrivals, which reads as a copy paste error and blurs which request station staff can actually help with in person.

findings.fix: Add a descriptive alt attribute, or alt="" if the image is purely decorative.
findings.violation: The image has no alt attribute at all, so screen reader users get no information about its content, and some assistive technology announces the raw filename instead.

findings.evidence: The document goes from an h1 to an h2 (s1-h) to an h4 (s2-h, "Accessibility improvements") with no h3 in between.
findings.fix: Change the s2 heading to h2, matching the other section headings, or insert the missing h3 level.
findings.violation: Skipping a heading level breaks the logical outline that screen reader users rely on to navigate by heading level.

findings.evidence: <table id="s2-table1"> with header row Zone, Status and no caption element.
findings.fix: Add a caption element, for example "Zone status", before the header row.
findings.violation: The table has no caption or accessible name, so a screen reader user landing on it has no way to know what data it summarizes.

findings.evidence: Local residents can check real time arrivals through the online portal. A confirmation message follows once the request is processed.
findings.fix: Add role="status", or aria-live="polite", to the status card container.
findings.violation: A region that reflects live status information has no role="status" or aria-live attribute, so screen reader users are never notified when its content updates.

findings.evidence: <div class="icon-delete" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-label="Delete item" id="s3-customcontrol">
findings.fix: Replace the div with a native button element, for example button type="button" aria-label="Delete item", containing the icon.
findings.violation: A clickable control is built from a div with role="button" and tabindex instead of a native button element, so keyboard activation with Space and Enter, focus styling, and form semantics all have to be reimplemented by hand and are easy to get wrong or omit.

findings.evidence: <div class="wizard-steps" id="s3-wizard"> containing three div elements with class "step": "Choose a plan", "Enter payment details", "Confirm your order".
findings.fix: Mark the steps up as an ordered list of list items and add aria-current="step" to the active one.
findings.violation: A three step sequence is marked up as plain divs with no list semantics and no indication of which step is current, so a screen reader user cannot tell it is an ordered sequence or where they are in it.

findings.evidence: "For the full list of upcoming adjustments, click here."
findings.fix: Reword the link text to describe the destination, for example "see the full list of upcoming adjustments".
findings.violation: "Click here" is not descriptive out of context, so a screen reader user browsing by a list of links hears only "click here" with no idea where the link goes.

findings.evidence: <label for="phone">Phone number (required)</label> next to <input id="phone" type="tel">
findings.fix: Add required, or aria-required="true", to the phone input.
findings.violation: The label text tells sighted users the field is required, but the input carries no required or aria-required attribute, so assistive technology never announces that requirement.

findings.evidence: followed by Enter a 6 character code using letters and numbers only.
findings.fix: Add aria-describedby="s3-form-promo-error" to the promo input.
findings.location: section s3 form, promo code field
findings.violation: The field is marked invalid but is not programmatically associated with its error message, so a screen reader user is told the field is invalid without ever hearing why.

findings.evidence: <button type="submit" class="btn-primary" id="s3-form-submit" aria-label="Send form now">Submit</button>
findings.fix: Remove the aria-label, or change it to include the visible word "Submit", so the accessible name matches the visible text.
findings.violation: The visible label "Submit" and the accessible name "Send form now" do not match, so a speech input user who says "click Submit" may fail to activate the button.

findings.evidence: <div id="main-content"> wraps the h1 and all three sections.
findings.fix: Change the wrapping div to a main element, or add role="main" to it.
findings.violation: The primary content of the page is wrapped in a plain div instead of a landmark element, so screen reader users cannot jump directly to the main content region.
